newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban threaten to hit back for Kabul bombing.
newsitem.headline: Taleban threaten to hit back for Kabul bombing.

text.p: KABUL, July 7 (reuter) - The Afghan islamic Taleban militia threatened on Monday to retaliate after opposition warplanes bombed Kabul for the third time in four days.
'We will take similar action should they continue to bomb Kabul,' Taleban spokesman Abdul Wak Mutawakkil said by telephone from the southern town of kandahar, the militia's headquarters.

Aircraft belonging to northern opposition leader general Abdul Malik have bombed Kabul three times since Friday, targeting the civilian and military airport in the northeast of the city and killing at least three Taleban fighters and wounding two.
An opposition plane dropped one bomb near the airport in the latest bombing in the early hours of Monday, causing no casualties, a Pakistan-based Afghan News service reported.
The Afghan islamic press said the bomb landed about two Km (a mile) southeast of the airport, setting a timber store ablaze. It broke windows in the Mikrorayan residential area.

'This type of bombing will only create anger and concern among civilians and won't make much change in our policy, ' Mutawakkil said, adding that the Taleban would bomb opposition military targets in the north.

He accused Russia, Iran and other unspecified neighbouring countries of proving Malik to carry out air attacks on Kabul and said he would not rule out the possibility that the bombers had taken off from airfields outside Afghanistan.
'Our message for them is to stop wounding Afghans and to ask their mercenaries not to bomb Kabul,' Mutawakkil said.
The renewed bombings have shocked war-weary Kabulis.
On Monday, people gathered near a four-metre (13-foot) crater caused by a bomb dropped on Sunday night in Mikrorayan.
'This time we were lucky, but that's not the end of the war here,' said Ahmed Gul.
Gul, in his mid-forties, endured factional warfare in Kabul for 4-1/2 years before it fell to the Taleban in September.
'My house was flattened in the war,' he said. 'We went to (the Pakistani border city of) Peshawar for a while but it was worse there. There was no job and it was expensive to live.'
Most parts of Kabul have been damaged or reduced to rubble in factional fighting since islamic mujahideen guerrillas toppled a pro-communist government in 1992.
Gul said he had returned from Pakistan four months ago with his family of five hoping, in vain, to find security in Kabul.
Gul said his children had not slept for fear of air raids. His neighbour had moved his family to their old house in the southwest of the city, which used to be a battlefront.
The taleban, who control two-thirds of Afghanistan, are fighting to impose their strict islamic rule across the country, but have failed to quell opposition forces in the north.
